summary: Describes an architecture for secure firmware updates on resource-constrained Internet of Things devices. Updating is essential for fixing vulnerabilities, and also lets operators change configuration and add features.

eli5.summary: Small gadgets need a safe way to get repairs, so this describes how to deliver updates without letting bad guys sneak in.

questions: how to securely update iot devices
what is iot firmware update architecture
how does a device verify a firmware update
subtitle: A secure architecture for delivering and applying firmware updates to resource-constrained IoT devices.

tldr.problem: IoT devices need secure firmware updates to fix vulnerabilities, but resource constraints make this challenging. Devices must be updated automatically without user intervention, and updates must be protected against tampering.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC describes an architecture where a manifest file signs and authenticates firmware updates. A status tracker tells devices when updates are available, the firmware consumer downloads and verifies the update using the manifest, and a bootloader performs secure verification before activation.
tldr.outcome: The architecture enables standardized, secure firmware distribution via internet protocols like CoAP and MQTT, supporting diverse hardware configurations from single-MCU devices to systems with trusted execution environments and multiple processors.

today: RFC 9019 is Informational, providing terminology and architectural guidance for IoT firmware updates. The IETF SUIT working group has developed concrete manifest formats and protocols based on this architecture.

sections.title: The Need for Secure Firmware Updates
sections.content:
Firmware updates are essential for fixing security vulnerabilities in IoT devices, but constrained IoT devices present unique challenges. Unlike laptops or smartphones, most IoT devices lack user interfaces and must support unattended updates. The RFC emphasizes that an update is essentially authorized remote code execution, so securing the update mechanism is as critical as the vulnerabilities it fixes.

An update mechanism must enable three things: fixing vulnerabilities with new code, updating configuration to adapt devices to new environments, and adding functionality to deployed devices. The challenge is achieving this while protecting against tampering and reverse engineering.
sections.eli5: Tiny computers sitting in factories need to get fixed and improved, but nobody can visit them physically. They need to be updated over the internet, and we need to make sure the updates are real and safe.

sections.title: Architecture Components
sections.content:
The architecture describes the key players in a firmware update: an author creates firmware and manifests, a firmware server stores and delivers them, a status tracker on both server and device tells when updates are available and tracks their progress, and a firmware consumer on the device downloads and verifies updates. A bootloader performs final verification and hands control to the new firmware.

Firmware images can be delivered as a bundle (manifest and image together, useful for offline updates via USB) or detached (manifest first, then image fetched on demand). The architecture supports any transport: CoAP, MQTT, HTTP, Bluetooth, or even mesh networks. Updates can be client-initiated (device polls for updates), server-initiated (server pushes to device), or hybrid (server announces, device fetches). Multicast and broadcast distribution is possible because security depends on the manifest signature, not on secure transport.
sections.eli5: Several computers talk to each other: one stores the updates, one tells the device when to check, one downloads the update, and one makes sure it is safe before running it. They can use any type of internet connection.

sections.title: Manifests and Trust
sections.content:
A manifest is metadata that the firmware consumer uses to decide whether to apply an update. It answers questions like: Should I trust the author? (using trust anchors stored on the device), Is this firmware for my device? (using Vendor ID, Class ID, Device ID), Is this newer than what I have? (using a sequence number), and How should I install it? (using commands that the firmware consumer executes). The manifest also specifies which firmware image to fetch and from where.

The manifest is cryptographically signed or uses a message authentication code (MAC) to prevent tampering. A Trust Provisioning Authority (typically the device manufacturer) installs trust anchors on devices before deployment in an out-of-band process. Complex deployments may require multiple signers: an author may create firmware, but a device operator must also authorize the update, so the device is configured to accept the update only if signed by both parties.

Manifests are transport-agnostic, meaning they work the same way whether delivered over CoAP, HTTP, or USB. This enables flexibility in how updates reach devices.
sections.eli5: The manifest is like a certificate that says "this update is real, it is for your device, and it is newer than what you have." It is signed with a secret key so bad actors cannot fake it.

sections.title: Hardware Configurations
sections.content:
The RFC categorizes IoT devices by their hardware to show how the architecture applies to all of them. A single MCU device has one microcontroller and must swap old and new firmware in place because the code cannot be relocated. A device with secure mode partitioning has one CPU that supports trusted and untrusted regions; firmware updates happen in secure mode and can update each region independently or atomically. Symmetric multiprocessor devices running Linux have multiple cores and can store multiple firmware images, choosing the best one to boot. Dual CPU with shared memory has two different CPUs sharing RAM; updates are coordinated to ensure consistency. Dual CPU with separate memory has each CPU responsible for its own firmware, coordinated through a primary CPU.

The bootloader must implement secure boot: it fetches the manifest from storage, parses it, verifies the digital signature or MAC using stored trust anchors, and only executes the firmware if verification succeeds. It must also handle decryption if the firmware image was encrypted for confidentiality.
sections.eli5: Different gadgets are built differently: some have one brain, some have two, some have lots of memory. The architecture works on all of them because the trust part (checking the signature) happens the same way everywhere.

sections.title: Protecting the Update
sections.content:
Authentication ensures the device knows who created the update. Trust anchors (public keys) are installed before deployment, and the device verifies the signature on the manifest. Integrity protection uses signatures or MACs to detect modification; the device must verify this before fetching or installing anything. Confidentiality protection is optional: firmware images can be encrypted so that reverse engineering is harder. Confidentiality protection must work with content distribution networks (CDNs) and broadcast, so it uses per-device encryption.

The RFC warns that RSA and elliptic curve signatures may become vulnerable to quantum-accelerated attacks around 2030. Bootloader code in read-only memory cannot be updated, so designers should consider post-quantum signature schemes like hash-based signatures. The manifest specification must support algorithm extensibility so that security properties can adapt as threats evolve.

The architecture also addresses rollback protection: a device presented with an old but validly signed manifest must not accept it, because vulnerabilities in old firmware could let attackers gain control. Sequence numbers in the manifest prevent this.
sections.eli5: The update process uses three kinds of protection: proving who created it (a signature), making sure nobody changed it (a hash), and optionally scrambling it so only your device can read it.
